the-work-of-the-surface.title: Six ways to read a surface
the-work-of-the-surface.summary: Find another face, follow a line of signs, look through carved openings, and watch a surface become space.

provenance.method: An AI-authored selection and reading sequence prepared from this exhibition’s existing captions and linked object records. This edition is prepared in advance; it is not generated during your visit.

the-work-of-the-surface.rationale: These six works make a small change of viewpoint useful in six different ways: several fronts, incised signs, layered materials, a curved picture, open metal lines, and carved stone. They form a looking sequence, not a claim that their makers shared an intention or influenced one another.

facts.text: This helmet mask has four faces and no single back.
Closely incised signs follow the curved wooden surface of this Rongorongo tablet from Rapa Nui.
The museum records 1,580 glyphs and notes that the writing remains undeciphered.
Carved and drilled ivory panels expose gold leaf beneath the casket’s stars and rosettes.
Overglaze polychromy and gold depict a courtly gathering on stonepaste.
Pevsner builds a curved surface from welded metal filaments.
The rough outer skin of the alabaster meets a precisely finished interior.

stops.title: Find the next face
stops.prompt: Drag to turn the mask slowly. Find a second face, then a third. Is there a view you would call the back?
stops.reading: Four faces give this helmet mask several fronts. Moving around it changes which face meets you.
stops.whyHere: A turn immediately changes what you see: a first reason to leave a single front view behind.
stops.nextConnection: Next, leave the recognizable face for rows of cut signs.

stops.title: Follow a line of signs
stops.prompt: Turn the tablet to follow a row of cut signs around its curved wooden surface. Use the zoom buttons to look more closely at the grooves.
stops.reading: The writing remains undeciphered. A clear model can show the marks without supplying their meaning.
stops.whyHere: Close looking has limits: seeing a mark clearly is different from being able to read it.
stops.nextConnection: Next, look through cut openings rather than along incised lines.

stops.title: Look beneath the carving
stops.prompt: Move around the lid and sides. Find a star or rosette where the carved ivory opens onto the gold leaf beneath.
stops.reading: Openings reveal another material below the carved panels. The casket’s surface is made in layers.
stops.whyHere: A surface can let you see the material below it, as well as cover an object.
stops.nextConnection: From a layered box, move to an image carried by a curved bowl.

stops.title: Tilt the picture
stops.prompt: Turn the bowl to keep its painted figures in view. Follow the scene toward the rim and notice how it bends with the container.
stops.reading: Paint and gold describe a courtly gathering on stonepaste. The image occupies a vessel, rather than a flat page.
stops.whyHere: The viewing angle becomes part of looking at an image.
stops.nextConnection: Now leave the painted image for a surface built from repeated metal lines.

stops.title: Look between the lines
stops.prompt: Turn the work and look between the metal filaments. Notice when they read as a curved plane and when they open into gaps.
stops.reading: Pevsner joins metal lines into a curved surface. The spaces between them remain visible.
stops.whyHere: A surface does not need to be a continuous skin.
stops.nextConnection: Finish with the opposite approach: a solid stone block shaped around an opening.

stops.title: Find where the finish changes
stops.prompt: Turn the alabaster block. Find the meeting between the rough exterior and the smoothly carved interior.
stops.reading: Different finishes give the same stone contrasting surfaces. Moving around the block changes the edge of the space within it.
stops.whyHere: The route ends at a boundary: where the stone stops, the opening starts.

the-work-of-the-surface.closing: You have reached the end of this six-work route. Keep one looking habit: try a less familiar side before moving on.
